question: With regard to the EU ban on the import and export of sealskin, we were able to establish a sensible Inuit exemption to ensure that sealskin can still be sold on the European market. The exemption applies when the seals concerned have been hunted as part of the Inuit peoples’ tradition, in a manner that meets certain animal welfare standards.

In the light of a response from the Naalakkersuisut (the Cabinet of Greenland) it is clear that, as they currently stand, the rules do not ensure that only people of Inuit origin can trade in sealskin. The Naalakkersuisut maintains that there is a lack of clarity with regard to how to check that the requirements of the Inuit exemption are being met.

Can the Commission explain how, at present and in the future, checks are to be made to ensure that sealskin sold on the EU market meets the requirements of the Inuit exemption, thus helping to safeguard the original identity and culture of the Inuit peoples?
answer: Regulation (EC) No 1007/2009 on trade in seal products, as amended (1) allows the placing on the market of seal products from hunts by Inuit and other indigenous communities, provided the specific conditions set out in Article 3(1) are fulfilled. Such conditions notably include the requirement that the hunt is not conducted primarily for commercial reasons, but rather for the subsistence of the community.
In order to be placed on the EU market, seal products must be accompanied by a document attesting compliance with these conditions, issued by a body recognised for that purpose by the Commission.

Such recognition is made in accordance with Article 3 of Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2015/1850 (2), which notably requires that such body has the capacity to ascertain that the requirements set out in the regulation on trade in seal products are met. Member States’ competent authorities are required to control and record the data included in these attesting documents.
So far, the Commission has recognised three attesting bodies: —
Greenland Department of Fisheries and Hunting (3);
Government of the Northwest Territories of Canada (5).

In its report on the implementation on the regulation on trade in seal products (6) published in 2023, the Commission announced that it would launch an evaluation (7) of the regulation on trade in seal products and of the Seal Pups Directive (8), to assess their effectiveness, efficiency, relevance, coherence and EU added value, as well as their socioeconomic impact and their impact on the seal populations within and outside the EU.
